blocks.x: Long explanations of why this thing makes it so much better this way, and you tell all the ifs, ands, and buts about it, but I don't know a thing about it.

George K. and I, John Steiner, are interviewing Roy Carew at his home, 818 Quintana Street, Washington, D.C., on June, what's the date? 21st. We've talked briefly before we began about some of Roy's reminiscences, and in order to make this a little more logical to the listener, we'll ask Roy to tell us where and when he was born, something about his family and his earliest

musical inclinations. Well, it's a long time ago. I was born in Michigan, Grand Rapids, and on December the 15th, 1883, and now in my 78th year, my folks came to Michigan from Canada. My father's father, having emigrated from Somersetshire in England to Nova Scotia, then traveled west to Ontario, and my father and the remainder of the family moved over into Michigan in the 1880. I grew up in Grand Rapids when I was 17, and in my 18th year, really, I went to New York for a season, got a job, and earned my living for a while. Went back to Grand Rapids, stayed until 1904, and went down on the Gulf Coast to visit my grandparents, who were living in Mississippi City at that time, my mother's father and mother. And I stayed there until September 1904, when I went into New Orleans. I went to work for the New Orleans Acid and Fertilizer Company, which was a branch of the Union Oil Company. The plant was in Gretna, Louisiana, and I worked at the plant for a couple of years. I went to work in New Orleans on Labor Day of 1904. I went down to the city office, which was in the Hibernia Bank and Trust Building, and waited in the office on the eighth floor, I believe it was, for the superintendent to come from Gretna, where the factory was located, and pick me up and take me over to my new job. I came, while we were waiting there, there was a sudden burst of music from Carondelet Street, right below the windows of the Hibernia Bank and Trust Company, and everybody went to the windows and looked out. Happened to be the Negro Labor Day Parade, 1904. That was my first introduction to New Orleans music, and I must say that it struck me as being very lively, good marching music. They were stepping along in fine shape down Carondelet Street. There were several bands in the parade, but I don't recollect much about them. But in as much as the year was 1904, and they've talked so much about Buddy Bolden being on the scene then, I feel that possibly he was one of the players, and his band must have been in the parade. And then I went over, the superintendent came along and carried me over to Gretna, which is on the other side of the river, opposite Jackson Avenue, New Orleans. While in Gretna, I got my first introduction to what you might call little blues tunes, speaking of characteristic music. They weren't good and they weren't complete, but the office boy, who was a white boy by the way, about 13 years old, must have heard his older brothers singing these little rye-balled strains. And well, they weren't all rye-balled, but some of them were rather rye-balled. And one of the first ones turned out later to go into the song, which was the Hesitation Blues. Hello, Central, what's the matter with this line? I want to talk to that high brown of mine. Tell me how long must I wait? Do I get you now or do I hesitate? Well, he sang that and a couple others maybe on that order. And he also had a fragment of what Jelly Roll wrote up later as Buddy Bolden's Blues. He sang it about Miss Susie. Thought I heard Miss Susie shout. Open up the window and let the breeze blow out. And he had any number of them. One that would go with Hesitation Blues was, I was born in the country, raised in town. I'm a backbone breaker from my navel down. Tell me how. I have to wait. Well, he sang. As I say, he must have gotten them from his older brothers. They were a hot bunch around there. But right across from the fertilizer office over there was the Chickasaw Cooperage office. And the bookkeeper over there was a very fine gentleman by the name of R. Emmett Kennedy. He was of a very old family around that side of the river there. Harvey, I believe, the family lived. And he was bookkeeper of the Chickasaw Cooperage Company. He was a bachelor. And he had a little, he rented a little, a little house, small house opposite the Cooperage Company. And he lived there alone. Well, he had one Negro servant, I believe. He was a musician. He had a grand piano in the place. And it was his hobby to get the Negroes in there in the Coopert Company. Any of them that knew any music, anything of that sort, come over there. And he would pick up their tunes and play them on the piano. And he arranged a couple of books of what he called mellows, which were their tunes. And he arranged the first complete blues. It wasn't maybe much of a real blues, but it was a blues tune called My Honey Baby. And that was afterwards published in a book called Mellows that he published.
The music as well as the words?

The music and words. And this was about 1904 and 1905 that I heard, heard him play that. And I had heard my, I heard the office boy that, that sang these fragments of blues. I'd heard him sing little parts of that. Oh, my honey baby, she can cook and stew. She's a good doing baby through and through, but she's got low down ways. And something of that sort, you know. But just little fragments that this office boy sang. But anyhow, in 1906, Kennedy gave a concert in Algiers. And he played the piano and his niece sang the songs. Of course, he played some instrumental music also. But he had several songs that she sang, and she sang this Honey Baby at that time. Honey Baby. And that, that was the first blues I ever heard. And it was, as I say, I heard it in 1906 when he had arranged it. Well, the question came up later about the early date on blues. And I wrote to Kennedy, who had gone to New York and was in New York, and asked him when, when he arranged that tune. And he said, well, he had arranged it several years before the concert that I mentioned in Algiers. So that would place it at least about 1903, which was an early date. Well, what is the title of it? My Honey Baby. Honey Baby. I don't think there's Ma there.
Honey Baby. As you remember, it was the familiar blues chords.

It had blues chords in it, blues notes in it. But it didn't stick strictly to the 12 bars. You might have, you might have called it a 14 bar maybe, or you, but it didn't stand strictly with that, the 12 bar as the, as it was afterwards the, the Orthodox real country blues was a 12 bar thing that they, that they held it to. But it did have the blue notes in it. And I asked him, I wrote Kennedy and asked him, he was in New York at the time, I wrote and asked him when he had arranged it. He said it was several years before he gave that concert. He had done it. He, he did it with the help of the man servant that worked for him, Negro man. But he afterwards published it. It's in a book of his called Mellows. Did you ever know Baby Seals? Did you see, did you hear? I didn't know Baby Seals, but he had a couple of pieces published in New Orleans, one of which was
called Baby Seals Blues, which was... Was that a, what you might call a traditional blues?

The first 12 bars of Baby Seals Blues, of the first 12 bars of the, of the verse, could be called a real blues. Well, it was, he was a vaudeville performer, wasn't he? He, he was a performer. I'm pretty sure he was anyhow, but he had two pieces published, or at least he had one piece published in New Orleans called, You Got to Shake, Rattle and Roll,
Or My Money Ain't Gwine. And then Baby Seals Blues.

The Baby Seals Blues he published later, but I'm very sure he got, got his inspiration around New Orleans because there's a phrase or two in the Baby Seals Blues, which, which were, were common around New Orleans. You see, I forget what they are right now.
What's the period of Baby Seals?

Baby Seals was around 1910 or 12, along in there, like 1910, I think, was the, the piece, so that you got to shake, rattle and roll that he wrote, and the other came along right afterwards, but it was published up in Missouri, as I recollect. I'd have to look that up. So then they, I'm off the track now.
Well, let's go back to Kennedy, following Kennedy's concert, 1906.
He also, he also played a couple of pieces on the piano that, as I recollect, they, they had blue strains in them, but I, I couldn't identify them at all. And, uh,
Now, how, uh, how were you able to listen intelligently to this music as early as, uh, 19, uh, four, 1906? You had an acquaintance with music before you got to New Orleans, did you?

Oh, yes. I, I had an acquaintance with it. They, they tried to give me lessons when, when I was a boy in New Orleans. They're not New Orleans, I beg your pardon, in Grand Rapids. They, they gave me lessons, but it was on an organ. And, and trying to pump an organ and, and, and play, it never, it never worked out with me. And I, I quit. Then they got a piano and I played a little bit, but I, I wasn't much on lessons. But I did pick around with tunes that I liked. And I, uh, I bought, uh, popular music. And, uh, at home we had the, uh, Mississippi Rag, which was the first ragtime piece published in the country. That was the first ragtime piece that got into print, published in Chicago. And, uh, we also had, uh, two or three other ragtime pieces there. Was that your interest, or, uh, someone else's? Well, I had two sisters that played, well, I had three sisters that played the piano really a little bit. One of them played right well, the other played popular music very well. And, uh, they, they were always buying new pieces. And they bought ragtime pieces as well as, uh, good music, you know, that is to say regular popular music, all kind of waltzes and everything else in that line. Were they older or younger than you? They were all older than I was. And, uh, one of them played the violin very well also. But they, they were very fond of popular music. They bought all the popular songs that came along that they could.
I don't think we got your father's name, your mother's, and these sisters.

My father's name was Robert Carew. He ran a shoe store there, a small shoe store there in the neighborhood where we lived in Grand Rapids. My mother's name was Rose, now, I'm getting twisted now, Carolyn, Carolyn, Carolyn Rose, uh, Rosely, Carolyn Rosely Johnson. Her name, her maiden name was. Her first name was Carolyn. And, uh, I had four sisters. And, uh, three of them played the piano a little bit. Two of them quite a bit, one just a little, and the third, the fourth, the fourth sister didn't play at all. But we always had plenty of music. My father played the violin and, uh, as a, like a country dance player. He played all the dance music like that. We used to have quadrilles
there at home. You looked at music as a, from a utilitarian standpoint. You looked at it to enjoy it.

It was our, it was our amusement at home, largely. We, we always had plenty of fun at home. We, we went to the extent of, uh, of getting a canvas covering for the parlor carpet, putting it on so we could have quadrilles there and dance on this canvas covered to the front room carpet. And my father would play the fiddle and we would have quadrilles there. And, uh, they were always playing. And, of course, when, when coon songs came along, ragtime coon songs, why, we were strong for them. We got them all that we could pick up all that got popular we tried to get. And, uh, so we had plenty of music all the time at home. And this one sister became a very good player. And she, she also played popular music. We, none of, none of them ever got, got, uh, too high tone to play good popular music. Did you have any mechanical music at home? No, we had no mechanical music at home at all. It was a long time before I ever had any phonograph in the house, even after I got to New Orleans. And, and still you were so interested in music that you'd pick up these coon songs in the ranks. Oh, yes. As they'd come out, we'd get them. If we went to a show and we heard a new song, we'd get that. And that was the way they were spread then, you know. I had a good summer resort near there in Grand Rapids called Ramona. And they, they booked vaudeville from Detroit and the east there. Had some of the best artists there and singers, dancers, coon shouters, minstrel shows came to town. And we were, we were very strong on that. Always went to the shows when we could. Bought the music if we liked it. If anything new came out in that line,
we got it. Well, you were pretty well acquainted with music before you went to New York then.

Before I went to New York, yes. But I kept it up there. I, I, I bought music there. I used to go down to Segal Cooper's was a very big popular department store then. And I'd listen to the demonstrations there and buy music then. And, uh. Did you hear any ragtime players in New York? No. Any of you recall? No, no, not, none in particular. They, they played, of course, they demonstrated the music at the, at the stores, played it there. But, uh, somehow or other, uh, they didn't have those ragtime concerts, uh, or contests, rather. It may have been early, actually. They came along. Well, they came along. You see, I was there about, uh, six months in the winter. I should have heard them. I used to go to Tony Pastures and to Keith's on 14th Street and Keith's, uh, Keith's 23rd Street and, uh, Proctor's, rather. Proctor's 23rd. There were three or four vaudeville theaters. I was very strong on, on vaudeville then. My ambition was to get into vaudeville as an acrobat. I had a partner that, uh, we used to practice acrobatics together. So I went down, we were going to New York and join a show or do something. I went down and got a job. I, I did it twice. I went down there and worked six months, two winters, 1900, let's see, 1901 into two, then worked the fall into three. Three, three, three and four, that's about it. And, uh, then I got back to, to Grand Rapids and my, uh, mother went down to, uh, to Mississippi, Mississippi City. My grandparents lived. And my mother went down there to visit, uh, 1904 early in the year. And I, uh, I quit the job I had in Grand Rapids and went down there to make a visit. And, uh, while I was there, I got the idea I wanted to go to New Orleans. I got a job in Gulfport for three months first though. And in September of 1904, I got a job in New Orleans and went there.

All right. That, that, that gives a pretty good background as, as to, uh, how you, uh, happened to notice the music that you were listening to. Now, uh, certainly, uh, people like Sushan tell the story from the standpoint of a participant. And apparently he was alert to, uh, the changes that were occurring from, uh, year to year in those early years. And I, I think that, uh, your stories might very well corroborate the many things he tells. Uh, you mentioned baby seals in vaudeville. Uh, there were an awful lot of, uh, minstrel acts and coon acts and so forth available.

The minstrel show was a very popular thing at that time. And for a number of years after that, I don't know when it began to fade, maybe in the early twenties, I don't know, or the late, uh, 19s. But, uh, but, uh, at that time, minstrel shows were a big thing. And, uh, they, they, you've got some very good talent in minstrel shows. All good talent of all kinds. They didn't stand strictly on Negro stuff. But, uh, there were, there would be acrobatics and, uh, singers of other types there, you know, different acts, comedy acts and that. And of course, they had the, the ensemble at first, and they sat, uh, around the semicircle and cracked jokes and sang songs and all that. Then they broke up and, and afterwards they had the oleo, which was separate acts. After the intermission came the oleo of these different acts, which could be anything in the line of entertainment. But they were a very popular show and they had some very fine artists in those days. And, uh, I was always interested in shows that I said I thought I was going to become an acrobat myself. I got pretty good, if I do say so myself, but I never got into business that the boy I practiced with that was going to be my partner, he stuck to it and he became one of the best in the country. He was an acrobat for, oh, about 10 or 12 years. What was his name? Harry Drew, his name was. And he, he appeared with a number of acts, the Glyn Ceretti family, Alion Pizer, and, uh, oh, I don't know, quite a number of acts he appeared with and got into burlesque with, uh, along with it all, and lasted a number of years. But he never knew enough to get a good night's rest. He would, he would go through the show, do the show at night, then he'd go and play cards the rest of the night somewhere, and finally broke down his health. So he died out in, uh, California in the early 20s, about 1920 and 21, I believe it was. So, uh, did I say that there was always music around home, popular music, and...

Well, uh, you, you heard Kennedy. Now, you, uh, also heard the street bands. Did, did you think that in these first years, 1904, 1905, or six, that you also heard theatrical, uh, music that might relate to the ragtime and the jazz sequence of events?
Well, the minstrel shows were always pretty strong on that.
As early as 1906, you heard minstrel shows in New Orleans.
Oh, before that, I heard minstrel shows early as 1900.
Well, uh, yes, uh, I, I meant in New Orleans, in the, in the, uh, in the birth grounds.

Uh, well, I heard them there in the, uh, as far as I know from the, from the first year I was there. They doubtless, uh, would come and play either the Crescent or the Tulane Theater. They were the two, uh, uh, popular theaters there. The, the Crescent was, uh, not quite as classy as the Tulane.
Do you think any of those shows, uh, were also the shows that you might see up in, uh, Michigan?

Would they travel that far? They would travel all over, yes. Uh, in, in New Orleans, they would always stay a week because they, it was such a big jump from another town that they, they would have to. In Grand Rapids, it was usually one or two nights stand up in Michigan. They wanted to split weeks or something like that. Yeah, split weeks. But down New Orleans, they would always spend a week and they would always, uh, have good, hot music. Trombone was a big, uh, was a big, uh, instrument with them. There's Lassus trombone that, uh, slide, you know, smear. They, they, I remember one, uh, minstrel show that came there, uh, gave a concert on Canal Street at noon. The band would come out and play at noon and, uh, they, they had no trouble attracting a big crowd there. And, uh, they had four trombones, I remember, in that thing, and they,

they, they really put it on. And... It's surprising what big bands they had. They, they often had a, uh, marching band in the street that would have two or three drums and choirs of, uh, trumpets and trombones. Well... And, uh, then a pit band, which might be a different instrumentation. Strange.

Oh, yes. Yes, that's right. They, uh, you, uh, in the, in the, uh, theatrical magazines of those days, the Clipper was the main one that I remember. The Billboard was more for sideshows in those days. The Clipper was the theatrical magazine, and I always took it. And, uh, there were always ads in there for musicians. Musicians that can drum, can double in brass, you see. They wanted, see, actor, or actors, can double in brass. They, they, they, half of the music, half of the performance, I suppose, went in the band, too. But when they, when they gave the show in the theater, why they, the orchestra would be the picked group, and the, the other fellows that usually were in the band, they were up in the, in the semi-circle there in the minstrel show. So they, they were very fine entertainment, too. I was,
I was sorry to see them fade away, but they did. Uh, were there such things as street singers

around New Orleans? Well, there were, there were, uh, I won't say that, uh, that there were street singers that merely sang, but there were, there were, uh, vendors who had a street song. They would sing now and then. I remember mostly blackberries, an old Negro woman that used to come around the neighborhood where we lived, and she used to blackberries there. I remember that, uh, somebody was, uh, trying to, to call to my sister one time. My sister was back in the house, and, uh, the neighbor wanted, had called to her, and she didn't respond. Evidently, she didn't hear. And the blackberry woman came along right then, and she, she saw this neighbor trying to call my sister. She says, uh, what are you trying to do? And said, the neighbor says, I'm trying to call Miss Carew to get her to come to the front. The legal woman selling blackberries, she says, I'll get her. Lifted up her voice and called, Blackberry! My sister went right to the front. Sister came right to the front door. She said, I knew she'd come out there. Well, I wonder, is that the same blackberry cry which they made into a popular record letter? Well, it could have been. I don't know, really. I'm not familiar with the record.

Oh, in, uh, the twenties, Paramount issued a record of street cries, which was a little strange, a folklore that you might not think they'd recognize them. But then, um, in recent years, a, uh, I think Harry Belafonte has made a, uh, Blackberry song. Well, there used to be any number

of different vendors going around them. There was the man that cleaned out the chimney, you know. Oh, yeah. They'd always wear them always wear them a plug hat along the outfit. I don't know why them chimney sweeps would have a plug hat, and they had a call. There's a story about the peanut bender song coming from an authentic peanut bender. Yes, they had, but I don't know about street singers really. Well, I wondered if they

collected dimes on corners or something of that sort. In Chicago in later years they'd go from tavern to tavern. Singers are small instrumental groups, and today you can hear them on Halstead Street and some of the places where there are open air markets. Set up a loudspeaker and a guitar. The one thing I remember

close to that is that at the corner Canal and Rampart Street there used to be a small open truck, one of these light delivery trucks with an open wagon. And they had a couple of pieces of music in that, and a Negro standing in the back or sitting in the back singing. They used to give a little concert there on the street like that, but it wasn't like a street singer really. It wasn't Clarence Williams and Pirone trying to sell their music for us. No, I never saw them. The messenger at the Custom House when I was working there in the 1916-17 would occasionally bring me in a piece of music that Williams and Pirone published. He lived, he was a neighbor of theirs out there. He'd bring it into me in the Custom House, music they published a little bit. Well, they must have been one of the early publishers. As far as that type of music goes, there were. Not that type of Negro music. There were, there was any music store in town, now and then would put out a piece of music. They'd have somebody get enthusiastic, you know, or compose a piece and come in and convince them that it would be a good thing to publish. And they would put it out. And, as I say, any, any store in town. Now, this Baby Seals, he had one piece published by Groove Wall there in New Orleans that was called Shake, Rattle and Roll. And you got to shake, rattle and roll or my money ain't wine. And the fellow by the name of Karoo got into D. H. Holmes and tried to persuade them to publish a piece, but the man says he wasn't publishing anything then. He carried, he carried me around to John Pewter and Pewter published my piece for me. So, that's the answer. What was that? The title of it? The title was The Full Moon Rag, or The Full Moon. And so Pewter put it out. He was very... What year was that? In 1909. Oh, yes. Would you like to see the cover?
Well, I have seen the cover. Have you? Yes. Someone in Chicago has a copy of it, and I think I've seen your... Is that Mr. Hardin or someone by the name? Yes, yes. You know him? Yes.

Well, I know he had it because he gave one to Jerry Heerman's. I believe he did at least. Yes, that was 1909. It would have been 1908, but he said, Well, here, it's pretty near the end of the year. Let's get a very good, fresh date on it. We wait after the first of the year. So, he published that. How many tunes have you had published? That's all. That one? Did you renew it a few years ago? No, I didn't. See? That showed how little I was thinking of that until Jetty Roll came to town. You did? I wrote to the library, not to renew it, but I wrote to ask them if I could have the copies that were deposited there, because I'd run out of them. And they never replied to my letter, but they just sent back my letter with the copyright date on it, just mailed it back to me. Maybe not taking time to read your letter and really understand it. Well, they wouldn't have published it. There's a strange thing about that. They wouldn't at that time have printed it for me, or given it to me. They leave the copies there as owned by the man that publishes them. Oh. Pewter could have gotten them. Oh, that's not. But I couldn't. Even after they expired. I think that you can get photocopies. Oh, yes, I did. I finally did. I gave all I had away, and then I didn't have any myself, so I got photocopies of it afterwards. Has anyone ever recorded it? No, I don't think so. No, I'm sure they haven't. Or is that good?

They recorded one of yours, Basin Street Stroller, and what was the other one you did? I didn't know. That was later. They didn't record that. Yeah, you did. I thought that the one out there in Portland, Oregon, what is the...

The Powell Powell? Fowler. No, I don't think he recorded it. He arranged it all right. He arranged a lot of things. I mean, the acetates of it, or... I mean, acetates, yes. I had two pretty good rags I wrote later that never got published. Fowler's arranged them for the band, but...
Oh, yeah, they were recorded up there. Weren't they by Fowler's band? Weren't they done in Portland?
I kind of think maybe they were. I'm not too sure about it. Fowler is the one that did that...
He did that album. He did that album. Yeah. ...in Album for ABC Paramount. Yes. Did you ever hear it?
Yes, yes. Good recreation. Yes, I thought so. The band sound, band form. Your writing has always been something secondary with you. You've never been in the music business as a profession, have you?

No, no. I always had other work to do, and it was always a sideline. Did you play with professional groups? No, never played with them. I just fooled with the piano, got to playing fairly well, and it was mostly for my own amusement. I never played for anybody. My dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
You were telling us about Eddie Grissel's place?
Yes, that was a barroom on Iberville Street, or Custom House Street, I should say, and I think at the Corner of Liberty there was a barroom.
I hope it's worth something to you.
The things of interest are these matters on which you have recall, and I was asking whether intonate singing you could identify what we call jazz singing today, a rhythmic phrasing.
Well, that would be hard for me to say because I would have to… Well I'll say that it fitted in very good with a good jazz piano that he played. Of course now in those days jazz piano had…
you

well just before we change tapes we're talking about your the years 1919 something that's sort of a new one you say you didn't get to know the white performers in the jazz idiom you did know the piano players but these white bands hadn't become familiar to you by name you heard about the reputation of the original Dixieland jazz band in the north no I didn't the the Dixieland

jazz band didn't exist as such in New Orleans that as I recall it now the the the Johnny Stein was playing drums at the Haymarket on Custom House Street and the Chicago man or his representative asked him if he could get together a few musicians and come to Chicago so he he then assembled these his first group that went to Chicago Johnny Stein and I hadn't heard of him although I knew where the Haymarket was and doubtless had heard playing in there but paid no great attention to it I will say that the that there were there was it's like the thing there was so much good around you could go here one place and you hear some nice playing travel along the next place nice playing scene there good playing and I heard a great deal of it here and there in the other place I don't feel that there was the

competition amongst musicians which was some sometimes resulted in battles of music and the evaluation of one man against another and so forth now we hear about that from musicians themselves could you see it from the outside that anything like this was happening no I I wouldn't see that at all the only the

thing was that the that the the Dauphine theater as I said they had a ragtime contest one time that was a contest that was won incidentally by a player that that I didn't think was the best ragtime player but he he played a very a very popular thing in that they played Dixie with one hand and something else with the other hand you know that the entertainers rag really is what what it is it's a very good rag part of it is Dixie with one hand and something else with the other hand two two well-known pieces and he won the contest the Claire played there and and so did kid Ross I don't remember the other players but they were a half a dozen or so how were the contests run a single number or two or three well no they they sat around in a sort of a large semicircle or on two sides the contestants and then they'd announce one and he would get up and play his particular specialty and then sit down and they they would judge it by the applause I guess as I recollect I went to see it and that was how it turned out but Claire I think the Claire as far as regular playing goes and then I was going to be kid Ross was a better ragtime player not as flashy and he couldn't play anything struck in the stage reality also but anyhow they they were they were piano players all over town you could hardly go to a party but watch them hear piano players and I was particularly interested in them because I used to pretend to play a little bit myself but not too much but what would it not too well would the contest be a one-time

segments.chapter: Early life and New Orleans arrival
segments.title: Opening: interviewing Roy Carew in Washington
segments.summary: Steiner announces the interview at Carew's home and asks about his birth and early musical inclinations.

segments.chapter: Early life and New Orleans arrival
segments.title: Birth, arrival in New Orleans 1904, first blues and Kennedy's My Honey Baby
segments.summary: Carew gives his family origins and moves to New Orleans, recalling the 1904 Labor Day parade, blues fragments in Gretna, and Kennedy's arranged blues My Honey Baby.

segments.chapter: Early life and New Orleans arrival
segments.title: Baby Seals and his published blues
segments.summary: Discussion of Baby Seals' published pieces, their date and New Orleans phrases, and a return to Kennedy's 1906 concert.

segments.chapter: Early life and New Orleans arrival
segments.title: Early lessons and ragtime at home in Grand Rapids
segments.summary: Carew tried organ and piano lessons as a boy and heard ragtime sheet music bought by his sisters.

segments.chapter: Early life and New Orleans arrival
segments.title: Parents, sisters and music at home
segments.summary: He names his parents, describes his father's fiddle, family quadrilles, coon songs and vaudeville shows at Ramona.

segments.chapter: Early life and New Orleans arrival
segments.title: New York winters and the move to New Orleans
segments.summary: Carew recalls hearing music and vaudeville in New York, his acrobat ambition, and how he came to New Orleans in 1904.

segments.title: Minstrel shows and his acrobat partner Harry Drew
segments.summary: Carew describes minstrel show format and his friend Harry Drew, the acrobat.

segments.title: Minstrel shows and bands in New Orleans
segments.summary: Minstrel shows came to the Crescent and Tulane theaters, with strong brass bands, trombones, and ads in the Clipper.

segments.title: Street vendors' cries and street singers
segments.summary: Carew recalls the blackberry woman's call and other vendors, while George K. mentions street singers elsewhere.

segments.title: Local publishers and publishing The Full Moon Rag in 1909
segments.summary: Carew recalls Williams and Pirone, other New Orleans publishers, and getting The Full Moon Rag published by Pewter in 1909.

segments.title: Recordings of Carew's rags and Fowler's band
segments.summary: Steiner and Carew discuss recordings of his pieces, including arrangements by Fowler's band in Portland.

segments.title: Carew as an amateur pianist, not a professional
segments.summary: He says music was always a sideline and he never played professionally; the passage ends in an ASR loop.

segments.title: Tape 1: Eddie Grissel's barroom
segments.summary: A brief fragment about a barroom on Custom House Street.

segments.title: Tape 2: jazz singing and piano
segments.summary: George K. asks whether the singing could be called jazz singing; Carew says it fitted a good jazz piano.

segments.title: Original Dixieland Jazz Band and white bands in New Orleans
segments.summary: Carew did not know the white bands by name, recalls Johnny Stein at the Haymarket going to Chicago, and sees no band rivalry.

segments.title: The Dauphine ragtime contest and New Orleans piano players
segments.summary: He describes a ragtime piano contest at the Dauphine theater, its winner, and how loosely organised New Orleans entertainers were.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and Tempo Music
segments.title: Cabaret singers; meeting Jelly Roll Morton in 1938 and writing songs with him
segments.summary: Carew describes cabaret singers, then reads of Morton and Tony Jackson in a paper, visits him in Washington, proposes reviving Joplin and instead ends up writing words for Morton's songs.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and Tempo Music
segments.title: Tempo Music Publishing, Clarence Williams and sales of the songs
segments.summary: They discuss the company name, using Clarence Williams as agent, print runs, sales of 300 to 500, and bands borrowing the music.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and Tempo Music
segments.title: Carew's idea to revive Scott Joplin's music through Morton
segments.summary: He explains he wanted Morton to play or arrange Joplin's neglected rags so they could be published.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and Tempo Music
segments.title: Morton's circumstances in 1938 and the Library of Congress recordings
segments.summary: Morton had not recorded for years and was struggling; Carew describes the Library of Congress project and Lomax.

segments.title: Lomax's book and Morton's missing touring period
segments.summary: They discuss gaps in Morton's story, his road band c. 1915-16 and the unidentified band named in Kramer's book.

segments.title: Morton's stories of the road and W. C. Handy's band
segments.summary: Carew tells Morton's tales about the grip full of money and Handy's trouble leading a band.

segments.title: Publishing more Morton pieces after his death and Lomax's book
segments.summary: After Morton died, Lomax asked to quote tunes, and Carew published Mamie's Blues, Buddy Bolden's Blues and others.

segments.title: Morton's estate and how Steiner met Carew
segments.summary: They discuss who runs Morton's estate, Hugh Macbeth, and how Steiner obtained the Library of Congress acetates through Carew.

segments.title: Sound quality and speed of the Morton acetates
segments.summary: They talk about the primitive equipment, clicking heels, and the pitch of Morton's voice on different reissues.

segments.title: Morton's voice and Tony Jackson's singing
segments.summary: George K. asks about voices that recall Tony Jackson, and Carew points to a few notes in Morton's singing.
